[L1] # SHIA-RAG: Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
[L3] > Project Type: Minor Project (M.Tech)
[L4] > Date: August 2026
[L5] > Author: [Your Name]

[L9] ## Abstract
[L11] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language
Model (LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking —
splitting documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys
semantic continuity, produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L13] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a
novel 8-layer RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection
of rooted trees where each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges
encode hierarchical (IS_A, PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L15] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context
selection under token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closedloop feedback mechanism that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy
Minimization for automated hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on
query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark
specifically designed for hierarchical RAG quality.

[L17] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with
claim verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based
on user interactions.
[L19] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, SelfEvolving Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing

[L41] ## 1. Introduction
[L43] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L45] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in
external knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L47] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L48] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L49] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L50] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L52] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental limitations:
[L54] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L55] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L56] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM
receives incomplete or incoherent context |
[L57] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations |
Token budget wasted on redundancy |
[L58] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at different
levels of abstraction |
[L59] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g., A
→ B → C) |

[L60] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge
from multiple sources |

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

2/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

[L62] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L64] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L67] Traditional RAG:
[L68] SHIA-RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L71] The system:
[L72] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L73] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L74] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive
depth
[L75] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence
constraints
[L76] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L77] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L79] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating
Systems → Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization
for AI retrieval.
[L81] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L83] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L84] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L85] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L86] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L87] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L88] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans
[L90] ### 1.4 Contributions
[L92] This work makes five novel contributions to the RAG literature:
[L94] | # | Contribution | Novelty Level |
[L95] |---|-------------|---------------|
[L96] | 1 | Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection | Incremental (Novel Application) |
[L97] | 2 | Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest via retrieval feedback | Moderately Novel |
[L98] | 3 | Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for hierarchy induction | Moderately Novel |
[L99] | 4 | Adaptive Depth Traversal via query complexity classification | Incremental |
[L100] | 5 | SHEF — SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework for hierarchical RAG | Incremental (Novel Combination) |

[L104] ## 2. Literature Review
[L106] ### 2.1 Related Work
[L108] #### 2.1.1 Flat-Chunk RAG Systems
[L110] The foundational RAG approach was introduced by Lewis et al. (2020), combining dense passage retrieval with
seq2seq generation. Subsequent systems — REALM (Guu et al., 2020), RETRO (Borgeaud et al., 2022), Atlas (Izacard
et al., 2023), and Self-RAG (Asai et al., 2024) — improved retrieval quality, generation faithfulness, and selfreflection, but all operate on flat text chunks with no structural awareness.

3/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

[L112] #### 2.1.2 Structured RAG Systems
[L114] Recent work has begun exploring structured retrieval:
[L116] | System | Approach | Key Limitation |
[L117] |--------|----------|----------------|
[L118] | RAPTOR (Sarthi et al., 2024) | Recursive abstractive processing — clusters chunks and generates summaries
at multiple levels | Top-down summaries only; no concept-level extraction or entity resolution |
[L119] | GraphRAG (Edge et al., 2024) | Builds a knowledge graph from text, retrieves subgraphs | No hierarchy; flat
graph structure; no self-evolution |
[L120] | TreeRAG (Concept) | Organizes documents into topic trees for retrieval | No formal hierarchy induction
algorithm; manual tree construction |
[L121] | HiChunk (LlamaIndex) | Hierarchical chunking with parent-child relationships between chunks | Chunks are
still text fragments, not semantic concepts |
[L123] #### 2.1.3 Knowledge Graph Construction
[L125] Ontology learning and taxonomy induction have a rich history in NLP:
[L126] - Hearst patterns (Hearst, 1992) extract hypernym relations from text
[L127] - Taxonomy induction (Velardi et al., 2013; Bansal et al., 2014) builds hierarchies from web corpora
[L128] - Knowledge Graph Embedding (TransE, RotatE) learns vector representations of entities and relations
[L130] However, none of these systems integrate hierarchy construction with RAG retrieval and self-evolution.

[L163] ### 3.1 Overview
[L165] SHIA-RAG is organized as an 8-layer pipeline divided into three phases:
[L167] | Phase | Layers | Mode | Purpose |
[L168] |-------|--------|------|---------|
[L169] | Phase 1: Offline | Layers 1-5 | Batch processing | Extract knowledge from documents and build the
Knowledge Forest |
[L170] | Phase 2: Online | Layers 6-7 | Real-time | Retrieve context and generate answers for user queries |
[L171] | Phase 3: Continuous | Layer 8 | Background | Monitor, collect feedback, and evolve the Knowledge Forest |
[L173] Additionally, Layer 0 is the foundational data model (schemas, types, database contracts) shared by all layers.

[L218]

[L220]
↓ Layer 8: Log, collect feedback, update forest weights

[L47] | LLM extraction errors propagate to forest | High | High | Confidence thresholds, human-in-loop review for lowconfidence nodes |
[L48] | Forest grows too deep (>10 levels) | Medium | Medium | Hard depth limit (configurable, default=8), depth

[L49] | O(N²) operations at scale | High | Medium | LSH for canonicalization, ANN for CPG++, batch processing |
[L50] | Cross-document entity conflicts | High | High | Evidence-weighted consensus voting, temporal versioning,

[L51] | LLM hallucination in answers | High | Medium | Claim extraction + evidence verification, confidence scoring |
[L52] | Cold start (new domain, no forest) | Medium | Low | Bootstrap from domain ontology (e.g., Wikipedia
categories) |
[L53] | Database sync issues (3 DBs) | Medium | Medium | Saga pattern for distributed transactions, idempotent
operations |
[L54] | Self-evolution reinforces wrong paths | Medium | Medium | ε-greedy exploration (ε=0.1), periodic weight
normalization, anomaly detection |

[L287] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L288]
[L289] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

13/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L290]
[L291]
[L292] Traditional RAG:
[L293] SHIA-RAG:
[L294]

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM
Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L295]
[L296] The system:
[L297] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L298] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L299] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive
depth
[L300] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence
constraints
[L301] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L302] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L303]
[L304] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating
Systems → Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization
for AI retrieval.
[L305]
[L306] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L307]
[L308] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L309] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L310] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L311] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L312] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L313] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans

[L374] Attribution strategy: Feedback applies ONLY to edges in the recorded traversal_path . This isolates
retrieval quality from generation quality.
[L375]
[L376] Safeguards:
[L377] - Edge weight updates use a dampened learning rate (η=0.02, small increments)
[L378] - Layer 7 verification metrics (supported/unsupported claims) are tracked separately
[L379] - Anomaly detection: if confidence > 0.8 AND feedback == "NOT_HELPFUL" , log a warning (possible answer
format issue, not retrieval issue)
[L380]
[L381] ### 7.3 Self-Evolution Update Rule
[L382]
[L383] After each query with feedback signal $f \in \{+1, -1\}$:
[L384]
[L385] $$w_e^{(t+1)} = w_e^{(t)} \cdot \exp(\eta \cdot f) \quad \forall e \in \text{traversal\_path}$$
[L386]
[L387] Where $\eta = 0.02$. Edge weights are clipped to $[0.1, 10.0]$.
[L388]
[L389]
[L390] import math
[L391] import random
[L392]
[L393] ETA = 0.02
[L394] WEIGHT_MIN, WEIGHT_MAX = 0.1, 10.0
[L395] RESTRUCTURE_THRESHOLD = 0.3
[L396] EPSILON = 0.1 # ε-greedy exploration rate
[L397]
[L398] def update_forest_from_feedback(selected_nodes, user_feedback, forest):
[L399]
f = +1 if user_feedback == "HELPFUL" else -1
[L400]
[L401]
[L402]
[L403]
[L404]
[L405]
[L406]
[L407]
[L408]
[L409]
[L410]
[L411]
[L412]
[L413]

path_edges = get_traversal_path_edges(selected_nodes, forest)
for edge in path_edges:
edge.weight = edge.weight * math.exp(ETA * f)
edge.weight = max(WEIGHT_MIN, min(edge.weight, WEIGHT_MAX))
edge.access_count += 1
if f == -1 and edge.weight < RESTRUCTURE_THRESHOLD:
flag_for_restructure(edge, forest)
if forest.total_queries % 100 == 0:
rebalance_forest(forest)
forest.total_queries += 1

[L524] ## 1. Introduction
[L525]
[L526] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L527]
[L528] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in
external knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L529]
[L530] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L531] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L532] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L533] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L534]
[L535] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental
limitations:
[L536]
[L537] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L538] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L539] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM
receives incomplete or incoherent context |
[L540] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations
| Token budget wasted on redundancy |
[L541] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at
different levels of abstraction |
[L542] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g.,
A → B → C) |
[L543] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge
from multiple sources |
[L544]
[L545] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

[L581] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L582]
[L583] ### 13.1 Summary
[L584]
[L585] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text
chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L586]
[L587] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — to the best of our knowledge, the first formulation of RAG
context selection as a precedence-constrained optimization problem
[L588] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — to the best of our knowledge, the first closed-loop feedback
mechanism that modifies RAG knowledge structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L589] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy
induction combining semantic similarity, depth, confidence, and type coherence
[L590] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation for hierarchical RAG
[L591] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for
hierarchical RAG quality
[L592]
[L593] The complete system specification covers:
[L594] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L595] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L596] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories
[L597] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L598] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L599] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance
testing

[L524] ## 1. Introduction
[L525]
[L526] ### 1.1 Problem Statement
[L527]
[L528] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has become the standard approach for grounding LLM outputs in
external knowledge. The typical RAG pipeline works as follows:
[L529]
[L530] 1. Split documents into fixed-size text chunks (e.g., 512 tokens)
[L531] 2. Embed each chunk into a vector space
[L532] 3. At query time, retrieve the top-k most similar chunks
[L533] 4. Feed these chunks as context to an LLM for answer generation
[L534]
[L535] While effective for simple factoid questions, this flat-chunk approach suffers from five fundamental
limitations:
[L536]
[L537] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L538] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L539] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM
receives incomplete or incoherent context |
[L540] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations
| Token budget wasted on redundancy |
[L541] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at
different levels of abstraction |
[L542] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g.,

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

32/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

A → B → C) |
[L543] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge
from multiple sources |
[L544]
[L545] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG
[L546]
[L547] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L548]
[L549]
[L550] Traditional RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM

[L551] SHIA-RAG:
[L552]

Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L553]
[L554] The system:
[L555] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L556] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L557] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive
depth
[L558] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence
constraints
[L559] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding

[L581] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L582]
[L583] ### 13.1 Summary
[L584]
[L585] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text
chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L586]
[L587] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — to the best of our knowledge, the first formulation of RAG
context selection as a precedence-constrained optimization problem
[L588] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — to the best of our knowledge, the first closed-loop feedback
mechanism that modifies RAG knowledge structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L589] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy
induction combining semantic similarity, depth, confidence, and type coherence
[L590] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation for hierarchical RAG
[L591] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark specifically designed for
hierarchical RAG quality
[L592]
[L593] The complete system specification covers:
[L594] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L595] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L596] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories
[L597] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L598] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L599] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance
testing

[L33] #### OCR Detection (Multi-Signal)
[L34]
[L35] A single heuristic ( text_chars / page_area < 0.1 ) is unreliable. For example, a page with only a large heading
("RETURN POLICY") has little text but is NOT scanned. We use a multi-signal approach:
[L36]
[L37]
[L38] def needs_ocr(page) -> bool:
[L39]
"""Multi-signal OCR detection — more robust than text/area ratio alone.
[L40]
[L41]
Signal 1: Text density (text chars / page area)
[L42]
Signal 2: Font metadata availability (scanned pages lack font info)
[L43]
Signal 3: Image coverage ratio (scanned pages are mostly images)
[L44]
"""
[L45]
text = page.get_text()
[L46]
area = page.rect.width * page.rect.height
[L47]
[L48]
# Signal 1: Text density
[L49]
text_density = len(text.strip()) / max(area, 1)
[L50]
[L51]
# Signal 2: Font metadata (scanned PDFs have no embedded fonts)
[L52]
has_fonts = len(page.get_fonts()) > 0
[L53]
[L54]
# Signal 3: Image coverage (scanned pages are large images)
[L55]
images = page.get_images()
[L56]
image_area = sum(img[2] * img[3] for img in images) if images else 0
[L57]
image_coverage = image_area / max(area, 1)
[L58]
[L59]
# Decision: OCR needed if text is sparse AND (no fonts OR high image coverage)
[L60]
if text_density < 0.1 and (not has_fonts or image_coverage > 0.5):
[L61]
return True
[L62]
return False
[L63]

[L68] def calculate_ocr_confidence(ocr_result) -> float:
[L69]
"""Calculate OCR confidence from Tesseract per-word confidence scores.
[L70]
[L71]
Tesseract returns per-word confidence (0-100). We:
[L72]
1. Get per-word confidences
[L73]
2. Filter out words with confidence < 10 (noise)
[L74]
3. Compute weighted average by word length (longer words = more reliable signal)
[L75]
4. Normalize to [0.0, 1.0]
[L76]
"""
[L77]
word_data = ocr_result.get('words', [])
[L78]
if not word_data:
[L79]
return 0.0
[L80]
[L81]
total_weight, weighted_sum = 0, 0
[L82]
for word in word_data:
[L83]
if word['confidence'] >= 10: # Filter noise
[L84]
weight = len(word['text']) # Weight by word length
[L85]
weighted_sum += word['confidence'] * weight
[L86]
total_weight += weight
[L87]
[L88]
return (weighted_sum / max(total_weight, 1)) / 100.0
[L89]

[L90]
[L91] #### Text Cleaning (Safe)
[L92]
[L93]
[L94] def clean_text(text: str, pages: list) -> str:
[L95]
"""Clean extracted text while preserving legitimate content.
[L96]
[L97]
Safeguards against false header/footer removal:
[L98]
1. Identify candidate headers/footers by frequency across pages
[L99]
2. Only remove lines that appear on 60%+ of pages (true headers/footers)
[L100]
3. Never remove lines that appear on fewer than 3 pages
[L101]
4. Normalize whitespace but preserve paragraph boundaries
[L102]
"""
[L103]
if len(pages) >= 3:
[L104]
# Frequency-based header/footer detection
[L105]
first_lines = [p.split('\n')[0].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L106]
last_lines = [p.split('\n')[-1].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L107]
[L108]
from collections import Counter
[L109]
header_counts = Counter(first_lines)
[L110]
footer_counts = Counter(last_lines)
[L111]
[L112]
threshold = max(3, int(len(pages) * 0.6)) # 60% of pages OR at least 3
[L113]
headers_to_remove = {h for h, c in header_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L114]
footers_to_remove = {f for f, c in footer_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L115]
[L116]
lines = text.split('\n')
[L117]
lines = [l for l in lines
[L118]
if l.strip() not in headers_to_remove
[L119]
and l.strip() not in footers_to_remove]
[L120]
text = '\n'.join(lines)
[L121]
[L122]
# Normalize whitespace (preserve paragraph breaks)
[L123]
import re
[L124]
text = re.sub(r'[ \t]+', ' ', text)
# Collapse horizontal space
[L125]
text = re.sub(r'\n{3,}', '\n\n', text)
# Max 2 consecutive newlines
[L126]
[L127]

return text.strip()

[L57] ## 4. Data Model — Layer 0
[L58]
[L59] Layer 0 defines the foundational schemas shared by all layers. The two core data structures are KnowledgeNode
(concepts) and KnowledgeEdge (relationships).
[L60]
[L61] ### 4.1 KnowledgeNode Schema
[L62]
[L63] Each concept in the Knowledge Forest is represented as a KnowledgeNode :
[L64] [matches 4-5 | match_lines 296,298 | shown_lines 291-303]
[L65] - parent / children are convenience-only fields derived from hierarchical edges. In production, always derive
these from edge queries to avoid update anomalies (e.g., parent field says NODE_100 but the actual edge points to
NODE_200 ). These fields MUST NOT be treated as the source of truth.

[L66] - confidence is propagated from extraction confidence, parent confidence, and evidence confidence using
topological sort (see Section 4.4).
[L67] - abstraction_level (0.0 = very specific, 1.0 = very abstract) is used by CPG++ for parent filtering.
[L68] - extraction_confidence (not shown above) stores the original LLM extraction confidence before
propagation. This is the immutable baseline.
[L69]
[L70] ### 4.2 KnowledgeEdge Schema
[L71]
[L72] Relationships between nodes are represented as KnowledgeEdge objects. There are two edge classes:
[L73]
[L74] | Edge Class | Structural Rule | Example |
[L75] |-----------|-----------------|---------|
[L76] | HIERARCHICAL | Must form an acyclic forest (single parent per node) | IS_A, PART_OF, SUBCLASS_OF,
INSTANCE_OF |
[L77] | SEMANTIC | Unrestricted graph (cycles allowed) | USES, CAUSES, DEPENDS_ON, CONTRASTS_WITH,
SIMILAR_TO |
[L78] [matches 6-7 | match_lines 906,908 | shown_lines 901-913]
[L79]
[L80] --[L81]

[L86] Input: KnowledgeNode[] (with raw relations) → Output: KnowledgeEdge[] (validated, scored)

[L112] ### 4.4 Confidence Propagation
[L113]
[L114] Node confidence is propagated from roots to leaves using **topological sort** (Kahn's algorithm) to g
[L115]
[L116]

python
[L117] from collections import deque
[L118]
[L119] # Confidence weighting factors (must sum to 1.0)
[L120] ALPHA = 0.4 # Node's own extraction confidence weight
[L121] BETA = 0.4 # Parent confidence weight
[L122] GAMMA = 0.2 # Evidence confidence weight
[L123] DECAY = 0.95 # Per-level decay factor
[L124] BASE_CONFIDENCE = 0.5 # Default for root nodes (configurable)
[L125]
[L126] def propagate_confidence(forest):
[L127] """Propagate confidence scores from roots to leaves.
[L128]
[L129] Uses Kahn's algorithm (topological ordering) to ensure
[L130] parents are always processed before their children.
[L131] Processing in arbitrary order would give children stale
[L132] parent confidence values."""
[L133] in_degree = {n.id: len(forest.parents(n)) for n in forest.nodes()}
[L134] queue = deque([n for n in forest.nodes() if in_degree[n.id] == 0]) # Roots first
[L135]
[L136] while queue:
[L137] node = queue.popleft()
[L138] if forest.parents(node):
[L139] parent_confs = [p.confidence for p in forest.parents(node)]
[L140] avg_parent_conf = sum(parent_confs) / len(parent_confs)
[L141] evidence_conf = (
[L142] sum(e.confidence for e in node.evidence) / len(node.evidence)
[L143] if node.evidence else 0.5
[L144] )
[L145] node.confidence = (
[L146] ALPHA node.extraction_confidence +
[L147] BETA avg_parent_conf +
[L148] GAMMA evidence_conf
[L149] ) DECAY
[L150] else:
[L151] node.confidence = node.extraction_confidence or BASE_CONFIDENCE
[L152]
[L153] for child in forest.children(node):

[L155] if in_degree[child.id] == 0:
[L156] queue.append(child)

18. confidence
Har Node equally trustworthy nahi hoga.
Example:
AI Diagnosis → 0.94
CNN → 0.98
Experimental Diagnosis Method → 0.51

Report me confidence propagation ka mechanism defined hai.
Node ka final confidence combine karta hai:
1. Node ki own extraction confidence
2. Parent confidence
3. Evidence confidence

Weights:
ALPHA = 0.4
BETA = 0.4

→ extraction confidence
→ parent confidence

GAMMA = 0.2

→ evidence confidence

DECAY = 0.95

Report ka formula:
final node confidence
=
(
0.4 × extraction confidence
+ 0.4 × parent confidence
+ 0.2 × evidence confidence
)
× 0.95

fileciteturn4file0L112-L157

36. Exception handling summary
| Problem | System action |
|---|---|
| Source node missing | NodeNotFoundError |
| Target node missing | NodeNotFoundError |
| Hierarchical cycle | CycleError |
| Multiple parent violation | validate_single_parent() |
| Semantic cycle | Allowed |
| Root node | Default/base confidence |
| No evidence | Default evidence confidence 0.5 in propagation |
| Arbitrary confidence processing | Kahn's topological sort |
| Parent/children inconsistency | Edge is source of truth |
Confidence propagation aur root/default handling report ke pseudocode me defined hai. fileciteturn4file0L112L157

[L60] A single heuristic (`text_chars / page_area < 0.1`) is unreliable. For example, a page with only a lar
[L61]
[L62]

python
[L63] def needs_ocr(page) -> bool:
[L64] """Multi-signal OCR detection — more robust than text/area ratio alone.
[L65]
[L66] Signal 1: Text density (text chars / page area)
[L67] Signal 2: Font metadata availability (scanned pages lack font info)
[L68] Signal 3: Image coverage ratio (scanned pages are mostly images)
[L69] """
[L70] text = page.get_text()
[L71] area = page.rect.width page.rect.height
[L72]
[L73] # Signal 1: Text density
[L74] text_density = len(text.strip()) / max(area, 1)
[L75]
[L76] # Signal 2: Font metadata (scanned PDFs have no embedded fonts)
[L77] has_fonts = len(page.get_fonts()) > 0
[L78]
[L79] # Signal 3: Image coverage (scanned pages are large images)
[L80] images = page.get_images()
[L81] image_area = sum(img[2] img[3] for img in images) if images else 0
[L82] image_coverage = image_area / max(area, 1)
[L83]
[L84] # Decision: OCR needed if text is sparse AND (no fonts OR high image coverage)
[L85] if text_density < 0.1 and (not has_fonts or image_coverage > 0.5):
[L86] return True
[L87] return False
[L88]
[L89]

[L95]
[L96] Tesseract returns per-word confidence (0-100). We:

[L98] 2. Filter out words with confidence < 10 (noise)
[L99] 3. Compute weighted average by word length (longer words = more reliable signal)
[L100] 4. Normalize to [0.0, 1.0]
[L101] """
[L102] word_data = ocr_result.get('words', [])
[L103] if not word_data:
[L104] return 0.0
[L105]
[L106] total_weight, weighted_sum = 0, 0
[L107] for word in word_data:
[L108] if word['confidence'] >= 10: # Filter noise
[L109] weight = len(word['text']) # Weight by word length
[L110] weighted_sum += word['confidence'] weight
[L111] total_weight += weight
[L112]
[L113] return (weighted_sum / max(total_weight, 1)) / 100.0

[L119] def clean_text(text: str, pages: list) -> str:
[L120] """Clean extracted text while preserving legitimate content.
[L121]
[L122] Safeguards against false header/footer removal:
[L123] 1. Identify candidate headers/footers by frequency across pages
[L124] 2. Only remove lines that appear on 60%+ of pages (true headers/footers)
[L125] 3. Never remove lines that appear on fewer than 3 pages
[L126] 4. Normalize whitespace but preserve paragraph boundaries
[L127] """
[L128] if len(pages) >= 3:
[L129] # Frequency-based header/footer detection
[L130] first_lines = [p.split('\n')[0].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L131] last_lines = [p.split('\n')[-1].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L132]
[L133] from collections import Counter
[L134] header_counts = Counter(first_lines)
[L135] footer_counts = Counter(last_lines)
[L136]
[L137] threshold = max(3, int(len(pages) 0.6)) # 60% of pages OR at least 3
[L138] headers_to_remove = {h for h, c in header_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L139] footers_to_remove = {f for f, c in footer_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L140]
[L141] lines = text.split('\n')
[L142] lines = [l for l in lines

[L143] if l.strip() not in headers_to_remove
[L144] and l.strip() not in footers_to_remove]
[L145] text = '\n'.join(lines)
[L146]
[L147] # Normalize whitespace (preserve paragraph breaks)
[L148] import re
[L149] text = re.sub(r'[ \t]+', ' ', text) # Collapse horizontal space
[L150] text = re.sub(r'\n{3,}', '\n\n', text) # Max 2 consecutive newlines
[L151] return text.strip()

[L258]
[L259] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L260] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L261] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L262] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )'
[L263] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L264] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L265] - **Default:** Paragraph
[L266]

Ye Layer 1 ka important exception-handling mechanism hai.
Maan lo:
100-page PDF

Extraction:
90 pages successful
10 pages failed

Success rate:
90 / 100 = 90%

Report policy:
≥ 80% pages successful
→ Accept document
→ partial_extraction = True
→ failed_pages record karo

But:
70 / 100 pages successful
= 70%

Then:
< 80%
→ Reject entire document
→ Manual review queue

32. Layer 1 me mistakes kaise ho sakti hain?
Ab ye technical analysis hai. Main report ke content se alag clearly bata raha hoon.

Mistake A — Hash exact duplicate hi detect karega
Same knowledge
Different PDF binary

SHA-256 different hoga.
So:
Semantic duplicate may enter

Report ki Layer 1 specification exact-content hash deduplication define karti hai; semantic deduplication yahan
specified nahi hai. fileciteturn5file0L41-L56

Mistake B — OCR detection heuristic perfect nahi
Even 3 signals ke baad unusual documents me:
False positive
False negative

possible hain.

First 5000 chars detect

[L35] ### 3.2 Data Flow
[L36]
[L37]
[L38] Raw Document (PDF/DOCX/HTML)
[L39]
↓ Layer 1: Validate, detect format, extract text, OCR if needed
[L40] Normalized Text + Metadata
[L41]
↓ Layer 2: Detect layout, segment into blocks, classify types, reading order
[L42] [Page → Region → Block] hierarchy
[L43]
↓ Layer 3: Split sentences, extract concepts/definitions/relations
[L44] KnowledgeUnit objects (candidate concepts)
[L45]
↓ Layer 3: Alias resolution (merge synonyms via MinHash LSH)
[L46] KnowledgeNode objects (canonical, deduplicated)
[L47]
↓ Layer 4: Validate relations against ontology, score confidence
[L48] KnowledgeEdge objects (typed, scored)
[L49]
↓ Layer 5: CPG++ → PRE → HV → FI → CLD (hierarchy construction)
[L50] Knowledge Forest (rooted trees + cross-links)
[L51]
↓ Layer 6: Query → embed → find seeds → traverse → Tree Knapsack selection
[L52] Selected context nodes (within token budget)
[L53]
↓ Layer 7: Build prompt, invoke LLM
[L54]
↓ Layer 7: Verify claims against evidence, bind citations
[L55] Answer with citations + confidence score
[L56]
[L57]

↓ Layer 8: Log, collect feedback, update forest weights

[L469]
[L470] The parser uses rule-based heuristics for block classification:
[L471] - **Heading:** Short line (< 100 chars), no ending punctuation, starts with uppercase
[L472] - **List:** Starts with `- `, `* `, `• `, or `1.`
[L473] - **Table:** Contains 3+ pipe characters (`|`) — uses regex `re.match(r'^(def |class |import |from )'
[L474] - **Code:** Uses regex pattern matching (NOT `"def " in text`, which falsely matches "definitely")
[L475] - **Definition:** Contains phrases like "is defined as", "refers to"
[L476] - **Default:** Paragraph
[L477]
[L478] #### Table Cell-Level Parsing
[L479]
[L480] When a block is classified as `TABLE`, the system uses `pdfplumber` or `Camelot` to reconstruct cell[L481]

[L88] + def tree_knapsack(root, budget, forest):
[L89] + """Select nodes maximizing utility, but a child can only be
[L90] + selected if its parent is also selected.
[L91] +
[L92] + NOTE: This is a greedy approximation (not exact DP).
[L93] + Children are sorted by utility-density and greedily allocated.
[L94] + Exact DP is computationally prohibitive for large token budgets."""
[L95] + dp = {} # Memoization cache
[L96] +
[L97] + def solve(node, remaining_budget):
[L98] + if (node.id, remaining_budget) in dp:
[L99] + return dp[(node.id, remaining_budget)]
[L100] +
[L101] + # Option 1: Don't include this node (or any descendants)
[L102] + best = (0, set())
[L103] +
[L104] + # Option 2: Include this node, then greedily pick children
[L105] + if remaining_budget >= node.token_cost:
[L106] + child_budget = remaining_budget - node.token_cost
[L107] + total_util = node.utility
[L108] + selected = {node.id}
[L109] +
[L110] + # Greedily allocate remaining budget to children by utility-density
[L111] + children = sorted(forest.children(node),
[L112] + key=lambda c: c.utility / max(c.token_cost, 1),
[L113] + reverse=True)
[L114] + for child in children:
[L115] + if child_budget >= child.token_cost:
[L116] + cu, cs = solve(child, child_budget)
[L117] + total_util += cu
[L118] + selected |= cs
[L119] + child_budget -= sum(forest.get_node(n).token_cost for n in cs)
[L120] +
[L121] + if total_util > best[0]:
[L122] + best = (total_util, selected)
[L123] +
[L124] + dp[(node.id, remaining_budget)] = best
[L125] + return best
[L126] +
[L127] + return solve(root, budget)

[L139] def estimate_abstraction_level(node):
[L140] """Multi-factor heuristic for estimating abstraction level of unplaced nodes.
[L141] Returns a score in [0.0, 1.0] where higher = more abstract.
[L142]
[L143] NOTE: Simple name-length alone is insufficient (e.g., 'A' → abstract? No).
[L144] We combine multiple signals for robustness."""
[L145] score = 0.0
[L146]
[L147] # Factor 1: Name length (shorter multi-word names tend to be more abstract)
[L148] word_count = len(node.name.split())
[L149] if word_count <= 2:
[L150] score += 0.15 # Short names like "Scheduling", "CPU" are abstract
[L151] elif word_count >= 4:
[L152] score -= 0.05 # Long names like "Advanced Encryption Standard" are specific
[L153]
[L154] # Factor 2: Number of source documents (more sources = more general)
[L155] score += min(len(node.sources) 0.05, 0.20)
[L156]
[L157] # Factor 3: Number of sub-concept hints (more sub-concepts = more abstract)
[L158] score += min(len(node.children_hints) * 0.05, 0.25)
[L159]
[L160] # Factor 4: Definition keywords indicating abstraction
[L161] abstract_keywords = ['general', 'category', 'type', 'class', 'family', 'group',
[L162] 'framework', 'paradigm', 'approach', 'method', 'technique']
[L163] specific_keywords = ['specific', 'particular', 'exact', 'instance', 'example',
[L164] 'implementation', 'variant', 'version']
[L165] defn_text = ' '.join(node.definitions).lower() if node.definitions else ''
[L166] score += sum(0.05 for kw in abstract_keywords if kw in defn_text)
[L167] score -= sum(0.05 for kw in specific_keywords if kw in defn_text)

[L159] > - Precedence constraints in Tree Knapsack: $x_i \leq x_{\text{parent}(i)}$ is unambiguous
[L160] > - Confidence propagation: single parent path, no need for multi-parent averaging
[L161] > - Cycle detection: simple ancestor traversal
[L162] >
[L163] > Multiple semantic associations are handled via `SEMANTIC` edges (cross-links), which are unrestrict
[L164]

8. Layer 2 ka actual internal algorithm
Report ka main pseudocode conceptually ye hai:
for each page:
segment page into regions
for each region:
split region into blocks
for each block:
classify block
assign ID
assign page number
assign region index
assign reading order
assign confidence
return all blocks

Report ke actual Layer 2 pipeline me bhi isi sequence ko use kiya gaya hai. fileciteturn6file2L205-L234

False code classification.

def
class
import
from

So:
def calculate_risk():

→ CODE ✓
This definitely improves...

→ CODE ✗

Report ke error-fix section me exactly isi false-match problem aur regex fix ko identify kiya gaya hai.

40. Layer 2 me possible errors

Error 1 — Heading ko paragraph samajhna

PARAGRAPH

❌

Impact:
Later:
Section context lost

Error 2 — Paragraph ko heading samajhna
Input:
PATIENT SAFETY REQUIRES CONTINUOUS MONITORING

But:
All uppercase
+
short

→ HEADING false positive.

2. Validate history

Bad segmentation:

1. Collect symptoms
Block B:
2. Validate history
Block C:
3. Run prediction

Kabhi-kabhi ye acceptable ho sakta hai, but agar list ek logical procedure hai to uski group structure break ho sakti
hai.

[L11] content:
[L12]
[L13] SHIA-RAG instead:
[L14] 1. Extracts knowledge (concepts, definitions, relations) from documents
[L15] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes (not text chunks)
[L16] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, siblings)
[L17] 4. Assembles context intelligently within a token budget
[L18] 5. Generates answers with citation-backed evidence
[L19]
[L20] ### 1.2 Why It Matters
[L21]
[L22] | Problem with Traditional RAG | How SHIA-RAG Solves It |
[L23] |---|---|
[L24] | Chunks break semantic continuity | Knowledge nodes preserve complete concepts |
[L25] | Duplicate/fragmented information | Entity resolution merges synonyms into single nodes |
[L26] | Fixed chunk granularity | Hierarchy allows multi-level retrieval (broad → specific) |
[L27] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | Parent-child paths encode reasoning chains |
[L28] | No cross-document fusion | Knowledge Forest merges concepts across all documents |
[L29]
[L30] ### 1.3 Core Innovation
[L31]
[L32] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "CS → OS → Scheduling → Round
Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization for AI retrieval.
[L33]

[L185] ### 3.4 CRITICAL: RBO Knapsack Ignores Node Dependencies (PDF 6)

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

202/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

[L186]
[L187] The Bug: The Retrieval Budget Optimizer treats nodes as independent items in a 0-1 Knapsack. But in a
hierarchy, a child node is meaningless without its parent context.
[L188]
[L189] > [!WARNING]
[L190] > Implementation Note: The algorithm below is a greedy approximation for the Precedence-Constrained
Tree Knapsack problem, NOT an exact dynamic programming solution. Exact DP for tree knapsack is $O(nB)$ where
$B$ is the token budget (potentially very large). The greedy approach uses utility-density sorting and provides a
practical near-optimal solution.

[L205] query_complexity: str # SIMPLE, MODERATE, COMPLEX
[L206] query_intent: str # DEFINITION, COMPARISON, etc.
[L207] seed_node_ids: list # Initial seed nodes from vector search
[L208] token_count: int # Estimated tokens in context
[L209]
[L210] class RetrievalEngine:
[L211] def __init__(self, forest, vector_index, cache_manager, config):
[L212] self.forest = forest
[L213] self.vector_index = vector_index
[L214] self.cache = cache_manager
[L215] self.config = config
[L216]
[L217] def retrieve(self, query) -> RetrievalResult:
[L218] # Step 0: Cache check
[L219] cached = self.cache.get_query_result(hash_query(query))
[L220] if cached:
[L221] return cached
[L222]
[L223] # Step 1: Classify query intent and complexity

Layer Explanation Plan

[L224] intent = detect_intent(query)
[L225] complexity = classify_complexity(intent)
[L226]
[L227] # Step 2: Embed query and find seed nodes
[L228] query_emb = embed_query(query) # Asymmetric embedding model
[L229] seed_nodes = self.vector_index.search(query_emb, k=5)
[L230]
[L231] # Step 3: Adaptive depth traversal
[L232] depth_config = {
[L233] 'SIMPLE': {'max_depth': 1, 'parents': True, 'children': False, 'crosslinks': False},
[L234] 'MODERATE': {'max_depth': 2, 'parents': True, 'children': True, 'crosslinks': False},
[L235] 'COMPLEX': {'max_depth': 3, 'parents': True, 'children': True, 'crosslinks': True},
[L236] }
[L237] traversal = depth_config[complexity]
[L238]
[L239] # Step 4: BFS traversal from all seeds
[L240] candidate_nodes = set()
[L241] for seed in seed_nodes:
[L242] candidate_nodes |= self.traverse(seed, traversal)
[L243]
[L244] # Step 5: Tree Knapsack selection (per-tree, then merge)
[L245] selected = self.multi_tree_knapsack(candidate_nodes, budget=self.config.token_budget)
[L246]
[L247] # Step 6: Assemble context (definitions first, then core, sorted by confidence)

[L198] ### 5.4 Layer 4: Relation Management
[L199]
[L200] Responsibility: Validate candidate relations from Layer 3 against the relation ontology, score confidence,
resolve conflicts, and produce final KnowledgeEdge objects.
[L201]
[L202] Input: KnowledgeNode[] (with raw relations) → Output: KnowledgeEdge[] (validated, scored)
[L203]
[L204] Pipeline:
[L205] 1. Validate relation type — check against ontology; if unknown type, attempt inference via LLM
[L206] 2. Resolve target node — map target concept name to a KnowledgeNode
[L207] 3. Check for duplicates — merge evidence into existing edge if duplicate
[L208] 4. Determine edge class — hierarchical or semantic based on ontology mapping
[L209] 5. Calculate confidence — weighted combination of source confidence, evidence length, and semantic
similarity
[L210]
[L211]
[L212] def calculate_edge_confidence(raw_rel, source, target) -> float:
[L213]
"""Confidence = 0.5 (base) + 0.15 * source_conf + 0.10 * evidence_quality + 0.10 * sim"""
[L214]

conf = 0.5

[L215]
[L216]

conf += 0.15 * source.confidence
conf += 0.10 * min(len(raw_rel.get('evidence', '')) / 200, 1.0)

[L217]

conf += 0.10 * cosine_similarity(source.embedding, embed(raw_rel['evidence']))

[L218]
[L219]

return min(conf, 1.0)

[L461] #### Alias Resolution
[L462]
[L463] After extraction, multiple KnowledgeUnit objects may refer to the same concept (e.g., "RR", "Round Robin",
"Round-Robin Scheduling"). Alias resolution merges them:
[L464]
[L465] 1. Build a MinHash LSH index (threshold=0.7) from concept names + aliases
[L466] 2. Find connected components of near-duplicate units
[L467] 3. For each group: select canonical name (most frequent), merge all aliases, definitions, properties, and
evidence
[L468]
[L469]
[L470] def alias_resolution(units: list) -> list:
[L471]

"""Merge KnowledgeUnits referring to the same concept.

[L472]
[L473]

Merge strategy:

[L474]

- Canonical name: most frequent name across units

[L475]
[L476]

- Aliases: union of all names and aliases
- Definitions: union of all definitions

[L477]
[L478]

- Confidence: average of unit extraction confidences
- Properties: merged (latest value wins, conflicts logged)

[L479]

"""

[L480]
[L481]

# ... build LSH index from concept names + aliases ...

[L482]

[L483]
[L484]

return [create_canonical_node(group) for group in merge_groups]

"AI Diagnostic Engine"

"AI Diagnosis System"

↓
Similarity / candidate grouping
↓
Connected Component
↓
One Canonical KnowledgeNode

26. MinHash LSH yahan kyun?
Suppose 10 lakh concepts hain.

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

236/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

Har concept ko har doosre concept se compare karna:
O(n²)

expensive ho sakta hai.
MinHash LSH ka idea:
Pehle likely similar candidates quickly find karo.

Then:
All concepts
↓
Likely similar groups
↓
Merge candidates

Report specifically alias resolution ke liye MinHashLSH(threshold=0.7, num_perm=128) specify karti hai.
fileciteturn12file0L57-L71

│
C

ek connected group ban sakta hai.
Then:
[A, B, C]
↓
One merged concept

33. Extraction Confidence merge
Report ke according:
Final confidence
=
average of unit extraction confidences

KU_2 = 0.80
KU_3 = 0.85

Final:
(0.90 + 0.80 + 0.85) / 3
= 0.85

36. Layer 3 me exactly kaunse algorithms/techniques use hote hain?
| Step | Algorithm / Technique |
|---|---|
| Knowledge extraction | LLM-based structured extraction |
| Output formatting | JSON |
| Failure fallback | Rule-based extraction |
| Concept creation | One KnowledgeUnit per extracted concept |
| Relation extraction | Candidate/raw triples |
| Synonym detection | MinHash LSH |
| Group formation | Connected Components |
| Canonicalization | Most frequent name |
| Alias merging | Set/union |
| Definition merging | Set/union |
| Confidence merging | Average |
| Property conflict | Latest value wins + logging |
Ye techniques report ke Layer 3 extraction aur alias-resolution sections me defined hain. fileciteturn10file0L36L86 fileciteturn12file0L49-L71

57. Layer 2 vs Layer 3 — sabse important difference
| Layer 2 | Layer 3 |
|---|---|
| Structure samajhta hai | Meaning/knowledge extract karta hai |
| Heading identify karta hai | Concept identify karta hai |
| Table identify karta hai | Table se knowledge extract karta hai |
| Paragraph identify karta hai | Paragraph se concepts/relations nikalta hai |
| DocumentBlock[] output | KnowledgeUnit[] → KnowledgeNode[] |
| “Ye content kya type hai?” | “Is content ka actual knowledge kya hai?” |

58. Final memory trick
Layer 1
DOCUMENT KO CLEAN KARTA HAI
↓
Layer 2
DOCUMENT KO STRUCTURE KARTA HAI
↓
Layer 3
DOCUMENT KO KNOWLEDGE ME CONVERT KARTA HAI
↓
Layer 4
KNOWLEDGE KO VALIDATE KARTA HAI

convert hota hai.

[L50] 11. Semantic Retrieval Engine
[L51] Input: Query intent, key terms.
[L52] Output: Set of relevant KnowledgeNodes.
[L53] Algorithm: 1. Concept Matching: Use the vector index to find nodes similar to query. Combine with
[L54] keyword matching: find nodes whose concept or aliases appear in the query. This yields initial node(s).
[L55] 2. Hierarchical Expansion: Based on intent, decide which directions to explore in the hierarchy:
[L56] Parent Expansion: If the query is general, include some ancestors of the matched nodes.
[L57] Child/Sibling Expansion: If specific, include children and siblings of the matched node. (For
[L58] example, TagRAG-style retrieval of tag chains【10†L185-L194】 suggests siblings may hold related
[L59] knowledge.)
[L60] Cross-links: Also follow CLD-related edges to capture semantically linked concepts (like LeanRAG’s
[L61] semantic paths【29†L37-L44】).

[L324] Cross-links: Also follow CLD-related edges to capture semantically linked concepts (like LeanRAG’s
[L325] semantic paths【29†L37-L44】).
[L326] Context Packing: Collect the text evidence for each selected node: e.g. definitions, example
[L327] sentences, and optionally a context snippet from source documents.
[L328] Budget Optimization: Solve the Retrieval Budget Optimization problem (detailed next) to pick a
[L329] subset of these nodes and their evidence that maximizes informational coverage under a token limit.
[L330] This process yields a Context Graph of nodes and edges relevant to the query.

[L639] Layer 3 / Layer 4 boundary: Layer 3 performs candidate extraction — it identifies entities, definitions, and

[L640]
[L641] #### Extraction Prompt
[L642]
[L643]
[L644] You are a knowledge extraction system. Given a text block, extract:
[L645] 1. Concepts: Named entities, technical terms
[L646] 2. Definitions: If the text defines any concept, extract the definition
[L647] 3. Properties: Key attributes with types and values
[L648] 4. Relations: How concepts relate (IS_A, PART_OF, USES, CAUSES, etc.)
[L649] 5. Domain: Subject area (e.g., "Operating Systems")
[L650]
[L651] Respond in JSON format:
[L652] {
[L653]

[L655]

[L656]
[L657]

"domain": "..."

"evidence": "..."}],

[L658] }
[L659]

[L660]
[L661] #### Alias Resolution
[L662]
[L663] After extraction, multiple KnowledgeUnit objects may refer to the same concept (e.g., "RR", "Round Robin",
"Round-Robin Scheduling"). Alias resolution merges them:
[L664]
[L665] 1. Build a MinHash LSH index (threshold=0.7) from concept names + aliases
[L666] 2. Find connected components of near-duplicate units
[L667] 3. For each group: select canonical name (most frequent), merge all aliases, definitions, properties, and
evidence
[L668]
[L669]
[L670] def alias_resolution(units: list) -> list:
[L671]
[L672]

"""Merge KnowledgeUnits referring to the same concept.

[L673]
[L674]

Merge strategy:
- Canonical name: most frequent name across units

[L675]

- Aliases: union of all names and aliases

[L676]
[L677]

- Definitions: union of all definitions
- Confidence: average of unit extraction confidences

[L678]

- Properties: merged (latest value wins, conflicts logged)

[L679]
[L680]

"""
lsh = MinHashLSH(threshold=0.7, num_perm=128)

[L681]

# ... build LSH index from concept names + aliases ...

[L682]
[L683]

merge_groups = find_connected_components(units, lsh)
return [create_canonical_node(group) for group in merge_groups]

[L22] ## 6. Online Pipeline — Layers 6-7
[L23]
[L24] ### 6.1 Layer 6: Retrieval Engine
[L25]
[L26] **Responsibility:** Analyze user queries, traverse the Knowledge Forest, and select optimal context no
[L27]
[L28] **Input:** User query string → **Output:** `RetrievalResult`
[L29]
[L30] #### Query Complexity Classification
[L31]
[L32] | Intent | Example | Complexity | Traversal Depth |
[L33] |--------|---------|------------|-----------------|
[L34] | DEFINITION | "What is OSPF?" | SIMPLE | 1 |
[L35] | COMPARISON | "Compare OSPF vs RIP" | MODERATE | 2 |
[L36] | EXPLANATION | "How does OSPF work?" | MODERATE | 2 |
[L37] | MULTI-HOP | "How does OSPF convergence affect reliability?" | COMPLEX | 3 |
[L38] | SYNTHESIS | "Summarize all routing protocols" | COMPLEX | 3 |
[L39]
[L40] #### Retrieval Pipeline
[L41]
[L42]

python
[L43] @dataclass

[L104]
[L105] For multi-seed queries, candidates may span multiple trees. The algorithm:
[L106]
[L107] 1. **Group** candidates by tree root
[L108] 2. **Allocate** token budget proportionally to each tree
[L109] 3. **Run** Tree Knapsack on each tree independently
[L110] 4. **Merge** results and trim to total budget

[L193]

[L195] - Edge weight updates use a dampened learning rate (η=0.02, small increments)
[L196] - Layer 7 verification metrics (supported/unsupported claims) are tracked separately

[L198]
[L199] ### 7.3 Self-Evolution Update Rule
[L200]
[L201] After each query with feedback signal $f \in \{+1, -1\}$:
[L202]
[L203] $$w_e^{(t+1)} = w_e^{(t)} \cdot \exp(\eta \cdot f) \quad \forall e \in \text{traversal\_path}$$
[L204]
[L205] Where $\eta = 0.02$. Edge weights are clipped to $[0.1, 10.0]$.
[L206]
[L207]

[L208] import math
[L209]
[L210] ETA = 0.02
[L211] WEIGHT_MIN, WEIGHT_MAX = 0.1, 10.0
[L212] RESTRUCTURE_THRESHOLD = 0.3
[L213]
[L214] def update_forest_from_feedback(selected_nodes, user_feedback, forest):
[L215] f = +1 if user_feedback == "HELPFUL" else -1
[L216] path_edges = get_traversal_path_edges(selected_nodes, forest)
[L217]
[L218] for edge in path_edges:
[L219] edge.weight = edge.weight math.exp(ETA * f)

[L223] if f == -1 and edge.weight < RESTRUCTURE_THRESHOLD:
[L224] flag_for_restructure(edge, forest)

[L83] #### 5.5.2 PRE — Parent Ranking Engine

[L84]
[L85] Ranks all candidates using a weighted scoring formula:
[L86]
[L87] $$\text{Score}(P, N) = w_1 \cdot \cos(E_P, E_N) + w_2 \cdot H(P, N) + w_3 \cdot \frac{D_{\max} - \text{depth}(P)}
{D_{\max}} + w_4 \cdot S_{\text{evi}}(P, N) + w_5 \cdot \text{Conf}(P)$$
[L88]
[L89] Where:
[L90] - $w_1=0.30$ — Embedding cosine similarity
[L91] - $w_2=0.25$ — Hypernym score (Hearst patterns + LLM fallback)
[L92] - $w_3=0.15$ — Depth penalty (shallower parents preferred; $D_{\max}=8$)
[L93] - $w_4=0.20$ — Evidence support
[L94] - $w_5=0.10$ — Parent confidence
[L95]
[L96]
[L97] def pre_rank_all(node_q, candidates, config):
[L98]
"""Rank ALL candidates, return sorted list."""
[L99]
[L100]

scored = []
for p in candidates:

[L101]
[L102]
[L103]

sim = cosine_similarity(node_q.embedding, p.embedding)
hyp = hypernym_score(node_q, p)
depth_score = (config.d_max - p.depth) / config.d_max

[L104]

evi = evidence_support(node_q, p)

[L105]
[L106]
[L107]

conf = p.confidence

[L108]

scored.append(CandidateResult(parent=p, pre_score=score,

[L109]
[L110]
[L111]

score = config.w1*sim + config.w2*hyp + config.w3*depth_score + config.w4*evi + config.w5*con
components={'sim': sim, 'hyp': hyp, 'depth': depth_score, 'evi': evi, 'conf': conf}))
scored.sort(key=lambda x: x.pre_score, reverse=True)

[L112]
[L113]
[L114]
[L115]

if scored and scored[0].pre_score < config.new_tree_threshold:
return [] # No acceptable candidate → create new root
return scored

[L118] #### 5.5.3 HV — Hierarchy Validator
[L119]
[L120] Validates that adding a parent→child edge maintains forest invariants:
[L121]
[L122] 1. Self-loop check — parent ≠ child
[L123] 2. Cycle detection — traverse UP from parent looking for child; if found, reject (would create cycle)
[L124] 3. Depth limit — parent.depth + 1 < config.max_depth
[L125] 4. Sibling coherence — soft penalty (not a hard gate); dissimilar siblings are allowed but penalized
[L126]

[L86] # SHIA-RAG: Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
[L87]
[L88] > Project Type: Minor Project (M.Tech)
[L89] > Date: August 2026
[L90] > Author: [Your Name]

[L92] --[L93]
[L94] ## Abstract
[L95]
[L96] Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as the dominant paradigm for grounding Large Language
Model (LLM) outputs in external knowledge. However, current RAG systems universally rely on flat text chunking —
splitting documents into fixed-size segments and retrieving the top-k most similar chunks. This approach destroys
semantic continuity, produces fragmented context, and fails at multi-hop reasoning.
[L97]
[L98] We present SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation), a
novel 8-layer RAG system that replaces flat chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest — a collection
of rooted trees where each node represents a concept (with definitions, aliases, properties, and evidence) and edges
encode hierarchical (IS_A, PART_OF) and semantic (USES, CAUSES) relationships.
[L99]
[L100] SHIA-RAG introduces five novel contributions: (1) Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context
selection under token budgets, ensuring hierarchical coherence; (2) Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest with a closedloop feedback mechanism that modifies edge weights based on retrieval success/failure; (3) Multi-Objective Energy
Minimization for automated hierarchy induction; (4) Adaptive Depth Traversal that adjusts retrieval depth based on
query complexity; and (5) SHEF (SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework), to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark
specifically designed for hierarchical RAG quality.
[L101]
[L102] The system processes raw documents through an offline pipeline (input → parsing → extraction → relation
management → hierarchy construction) and serves queries through an online pipeline (retrieval → generation with
claim verification). A continuous operations layer closes the feedback loop by updating the Knowledge Forest based
on user interactions.
[L103]
[L104] Keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Knowledge Graph, Hierarchy Induction, Tree Knapsack, SelfEvolving Knowledge Systems, Natural Language Processing
[L105]

[L228] ### 8.4 Novelty 4: Adaptive Depth Traversal via Query Complexity Classification
[L229]
[L230] Existing approach: All RAG systems retrieve a fixed number of chunks/nodes regardless of query complexity.
[L231]
[L232] SHIA-RAG approach: A query complexity classifier that dynamically adjusts traversal depth:
[L233]
[L234] | Query Type | Example | Traversal Strategy |
[L235] |------------|---------|-------------------|
[L236] | DEFINITION | "What is OSPF?" | Shallow: Target node + parent only (depth=1) |
[L237] | COMPARISON | "Compare OSPF vs RIP" | Medium: Multiple subtrees, sibling links (depth=2) |
[L238] | MULTI-HOP | "How does OSPF convergence affect reliability?" | Deep: Full path traversal + cross-links
(depth=3+) |
[L239] | SYNTHESIS | "Summarize all routing protocols" | Breadth: Root-level retrieval, expand selectively |
[L240]
[L241] Novelty level: Incremental — novel in the specific application to hierarchical RAG traversal depth.
[L242]
[L243] --[L244]
[L245] ### 8.5 Novelty 5: SHEF — SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework
[L246]

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

328/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

[L247] Existing approach: Standard RAG benchmarks (MS MARCO, NaturalQuestions) only measure flat retrieval. No
benchmark tests hierarchical retrieval quality.
[L248]
[L249] SHIA-RAG approach: A novel evaluation framework with 3 metric categories:
[L250]
[L251] #### A. Retrieval Metrics
[L252] | Metric | Formula | What It Measures |
[L253] |--------|---------|-----------------|
[L254] | Hop Accuracy | correct multi-hop answers / total multi-hop queries | Multi-hop reasoning quality |
[L255] | Ancestor Recall | retrieved ancestors ∩ gold ancestors / gold ancestors | Correct concept chain retrieval |
[L256] | Context Coherence | Avg semantic similarity between consecutive context nodes | Logical coherence of
assembled context |
[L257]
[L258] #### B. Hierarchy Metrics
[L259] | Metric | Formula | What It Measures |
[L260] |--------|---------|-----------------|
[L261] | Parent Assignment Accuracy | correctly placed nodes / total nodes | Quality of hierarchy induction |
[L262] | Tree Edit Distance | Normalized TED vs gold taxonomy | Structural similarity to human taxonomy |
[L263] | Depth Distribution Score | KL-divergence from ideal depth distribution | Tree balance |
[L264]
[L265] #### C. Forest Quality Metrics
[L266] | Metric | Formula | What It Measures |
[L267] |--------|---------|-----------------|
[L268] | Cross-Doc Fusion Accuracy | correctly merged nodes / total mergeable pairs | Entity resolution quality |
[L269] | Orphan Rate | root nodes without children / total root nodes | Isolated concept rate |
[L270] | Forest Density | edges / nodes | Knowledge forest connectivity |
[L271]
[L272] Novelty level: Incremental (Novel Combination) — to the best of our knowledge, the first benchmark
specifically designed for hierarchical RAG quality.
[L273]

[L484] votes = defaultdict(float)
[L485] evidence_pool = defaultdict(list)
[L486] for edge in edges:
[L487] weight = edge.confidence * len(edge.evidence)
[L488] votes[edge.relation_type] += weight
[L489] evidence_pool[edge.relation_type].extend(edge.evidence)
[L490]
[L491] # Select winning relation type
[L492] winner = max(votes, key=votes.get)
[L493]
[L494] # Log conflict if close contest
[L495] sorted_votes = sorted(votes.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
[L496] if len(sorted_votes) > 1:
[L497] margin = sorted_votes[0][1] - sorted_votes[1][1]
[L498] if margin < 0.2: # Close contest
[L499] log_conflict(src, tgt, sorted_votes) # Queue for manual review
[L500]
[L501] winning_edge = edges[0]
[L502] winning_edge.relation_type = winner
[L503] winning_edge.evidence = evidence_pool[winner]
[L504] winning_edge.confidence = calculate_edge_confidence_from_evidence(evidence_pool[winner])
[L505] winning_edge.metadata['conflict_resolved'] = True

[L654] | Problem | Description | Impact |
[L655] |---------|-------------|--------|
[L656] | Broken semantic continuity | Fixed-size splits cut across paragraphs, definitions, and logical units | LLM
receives incomplete or incoherent context |
[L657] | Duplicate/fragmented information | The same concept may appear in multiple chunks with slight variations
| Token budget wasted on redundancy |
[L658] | Fixed granularity | All chunks are the same size regardless of content complexity | Cannot retrieve at
different levels of abstraction |
[L659] | Weak multi-hop reasoning | No explicit connections between chunks | Cannot follow reasoning chains (e.g.,
A → B → C) |
[L660] | No cross-document fusion | Chunks from different documents are independent | Cannot merge knowledge
from multiple sources |

[L662] ### 1.2 Proposed Solution: SHIA-RAG

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

[L663]
[L664] SHIA-RAG (Semantic Hierarchy Induction Architecture for Retrieval-Augmented Generation) addresses all five
limitations by replacing flat text chunks with a structured Knowledge Forest:
[L665]
[L666]
[L667] Traditional RAG:

Document → [Chunk₁, Chunk₂, ..., Chunkₙ] → Top-k → LLM

[L668] SHIA-RAG:
[L669]

Document → Knowledge Forest (concepts + relations) → Adaptive Traversal → LLM

[L670]
[L671] The system:
[L672] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L673] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L674] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive
depth
[L675] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence
constraints
[L676] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L677] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L678]
[L679] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating
Systems → Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization
for AI retrieval.
[L680]
[L681] ### 1.3 Objectives
[L682]
[L683] 1. Design a complete 8-layer architecture for hierarchical RAG
[L684] 2. Define algorithms for automated hierarchy induction (CPG++, PRE, HV, FI, CLD)
[L685] 3. Implement a self-evolving feedback loop that improves retrieval quality over time
[L686] 4. Create a context selection algorithm that respects hierarchical constraints (Tree Knapsack)
[L687] 5. Develop an evaluation framework (SHEF) specifically for hierarchical RAG quality
[L688] 6. Provide a fully implementable specification with schemas, pseudocode, and deployment plans
[L689]
[L690] ### 1.4 Contributions
[L691]
[L692] This work makes five novel contributions to the RAG literature:
[L693]
[L694] | # | Contribution | Novelty Level |
[L695] |---|-------------|---------------|
[L696] | 1 | Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack for context selection | Incremental (Novel Application) |
[L697] | 2 | Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest via retrieval feedback | Moderately Novel |
[L698] | 3 | Multi-Objective Energy Minimization for hierarchy induction | Moderately Novel |
[L699] | 4 | Adaptive Depth Traversal via query complexity classification | Incremental |
[L700] | 5 | SHEF — SHIA-RAG Evaluation Framework for hierarchical RAG | Incremental (Novel Combination) |

[L33] def clean_text(text: str, pages: list) -> str:
[L34] """Clean extracted text while preserving legitimate content.
[L35]
[L36] Safeguards against false header/footer removal:
[L37] 1. Identify candidate headers/footers by frequency across pages
[L38] 2. Only remove lines that appear on 60%+ of pages (true headers/footers)
[L39] 3. Never remove lines that appear on fewer than 3 pages
[L40] 4. Normalize whitespace but preserve paragraph boundaries
[L41] """
[L42] if len(pages) >= 3:
[L43] # Frequency-based header/footer detection
[L44] first_lines = [p.split('\n')[0].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L45] last_lines = [p.split('\n')[-1].strip() for p in pages if p.strip()]
[L46]
[L47] from collections import Counter
[L48] header_counts = Counter(first_lines)
[L49] footer_counts = Counter(last_lines)
[L50]
[L51] threshold = max(3, int(len(pages) 0.6)) # 60% of pages OR at least 3
[L52] headers_to_remove = {h for h, c in header_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L53] footers_to_remove = {f for f, c in footer_counts.items() if c >= threshold}
[L54]
[L55] lines = text.split('\n')
[L56] lines = [l for l in lines
[L57] if l.strip() not in headers_to_remove
[L58] and l.strip() not in footers_to_remove]
[L59] text = '\n'.join(lines)
[L60]
[L61] # Normalize whitespace (preserve paragraph breaks)
[L62] import re
[L63] text = re.sub(r'[ \t]+', ' ', text) # Collapse horizontal space

[L134] def estimate_abstraction_level(node) -> float:
[L135]

"""Multi-factor heuristic for estimating abstraction level of unplaced nodes.

[L136]
[L137]

[L138]

[L141]
[L142]

[L143]

[L144]
[L145]

score += 0.15

[L146]
[L147]

score -= 0.05

[L148]
[L149]
[L150]

[L151]
[L152]
[L153]

[L154]
[L155]

[L156]

[L157]
[L158]

'framework', 'paradigm', 'approach', 'method']
specific_keywords = ['specific', 'particular', 'instance', 'example',

[L159]

'implementation', 'variant', 'version']

[L160]
[L161]

defn_text = ' '.join(node.definitions).lower() if node.definitions else ''
score += sum(0.05 for kw in abstract_keywords if kw in defn_text)

[L162]
[L163]

score -= sum(0.05 for kw in specific_keywords if kw in defn_text)

[L164]

[L165]
[L166]

[L170]
[L171]
[L172]

score = 0.5 * score + 0.5 * llm_score
return max(0.0, min(score, 1.0))

[L177] #### 5.5.2 PRE — Parent Ranking Engine
[L178]
[L179] Ranks all candidates using a weighted scoring formula:
[L180]
[L181] $$\text{Score}(P, N) = w_1 \cdot \cos(E_P, E_N) + w_2 \cdot H(P, N) + w_3 \cdot \frac{D_{\max} - \text{depth}
(P)}{D_{\max}} + w_4 \cdot S_{\text{evi}}(P, N) + w_5 \cdot \text{Conf}(P)$$
[L182]
[L183] Where:
[L184] - $w_1=0.30$ — Embedding cosine similarity
[L185] - $w_2=0.25$ — Hypernym score (Hearst patterns + LLM fallback)
[L186] - $w_3=0.15$ — Depth penalty (shallower parents preferred; $D_{\max}=8$)
[L187] - $w_4=0.20$ — Evidence support
[L188] - $w_5=0.10$ — Parent confidence

44. Layer 5 ka complete pseudocode
Report ke described components ko combine karke complete flow:
FOR each new node N:
# 1. CPG++
candidates = generate_candidate_parents(N)
# 2. PRE
ranked_candidates = rank_all_candidates(N, candidates)
# If no candidate reaches threshold
IF ranked_candidates is empty:
insert N as NEW ROOT
ELSE:
# 3 + 4
FOR candidate P in ranked_candidates:
# HV
IF hierarchy_is_valid(P, N):
# FI
insert P → N
assign parent
assign depth
propagate confidence
BREAK
# No candidate passed
IF N not inserted:
insert N as NEW ROOT
# 5. CLD
discover semantic cross-links for N
RETURN Knowledge Forest

Ye report ke 5-stage pipeline aur FI fallback logic ka integrated representation hai. fileciteturn20file0L77-L91
fileciteturn20file0L221-L264

[L366] ## 13. Conclusion & Future Work
[L367]
[L368] ### 13.1 Summary
[L369]
[L370] This report presents SHIA-RAG, a novel 8-layer Retrieval-Augmented Generation system that replaces flat text
chunks with a dynamically constructed Knowledge Forest. The system introduces five novel contributions:
[L371]
[L372] 1. Precedence-Constrained Tree Knapsack — the first formulation of RAG context selection as a precedenceconstrained optimization problem
[L373] 2. Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest — the first closed-loop feedback mechanism that modifies RAG
knowledge structures based on retrieval success/failure
[L374] 3. Multi-Objective Energy Minimization — a formal optimization framework for automated hierarchy
induction
[L375] 4. Adaptive Depth Traversal — query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation
[L376] 5. SHEF Evaluation Framework — the first benchmark specifically designed for hierarchical RAG quality
[L377]
[L378] The complete system specification covers:
[L379] - 9 layers (Layer 0-8) with schemas, algorithms, pseudocode, and inter-layer data contracts
[L380] - 12 defined functions with complete implementations
[L381] - 12 relation types across 4 hierarchical and 8 semantic categories

blob:https://chatgpt.com/e2b31603-f9df-4055-82cd-e524a077a7c4

408/678

03/09/2026, 14:50

Layer Explanation Plan

[L382] - 8 schemas covering all data objects from document blocks to query logs
[L383] - A 6-month implementation roadmap with technology stack, folder structure, and CI/CD pipeline
[L384] - A comprehensive evaluation plan with datasets, baselines, ablation studies, and statistical significance
testing
[L385]
[L386] ### 13.2 Key Novelties
[L387]
[L388] | # | Novelty | Level | Why It's New |
[L389] |---|---------|-------|---------|
[L390] | 1 | Tree Knapsack for Context Selection | Incremental (Novel Application) | First RAG system to formulate
context selection as a precedence-constrained optimization |
[L391] | 2 | Self-Evolving Knowledge Forest | Moderately Novel | First closed-loop feedback mechanism that
modifies RAG knowledge structures |
[L392] | 3 | Multi-Objective Energy Minimization | Moderately Novel | First formal multi-objective optimization for
hierarchy induction in RAG |
[L393] | 4 | Adaptive Depth Traversal | Incremental | First query-complexity-aware retrieval depth adaptation in
hierarchical RAG |
[L394] | 5 | SHEF Evaluation Framework | Incremental (Novel Combination) | First benchmark specifically designed
for hierarchical RAG quality |
[L395]

[L748] For multi-seed queries, candidates may span multiple trees. The algorithm:
[L749]
[L750] 1. Group candidates by tree root
[L751] 2. Allocate token budget proportionally to each tree
[L752] 3. Run Tree Knapsack on each tree independently
[L753] 4. Merge results and trim to total budget
[L754]
[L755] ```python
[L756] def multi_tree_knapsack(self, candidate_nodes, budget):
[L757] tree_groups = {}
[L758] for node in candidate_nodes:
[L759] root = self.forest.find_root(node)
[L760] tree_groups.setdefault(root.id, []).append(node)
[L761]
[L762] all_selected = []
[L763] for root_id, nodes in tree_groups.items():
[L764] tree_budget = int(budget * len(nodes) / max(len(candidate_nodes), 1))
[L765] _, selected = tree_knapsack(self.forest.get_node(root_id), tree_budget, self.

[L93] def multi_tree_knapsack(self, candidate_nodes, budget):
[L94] """Apply Tree Knapsack per distinct tree, then merge results.
[L95]
[L96] For multi-seed queries, candidates may span multiple trees.
[L97] We optimize each tree independently, then merge within budget.
[L98]
[L99] Note: Semantic cross-linked nodes do NOT require their
[L100] semantic predecessors to be selected (only hierarchical
[L101] parent constraints apply).
[L102] """

[L42] def assemble_context(self, selected_nodes, intent):
[L43] """Assemble selected nodes into ordered context string.
[L44]
[L45] Order: definitions first, then core concepts, then related evidence.

[L63] block += f"\nSource: {node.evidence[0].source_doc if node.evidence else 'N/A'}, Page {node.evidence[0].page if
node.evidence else 'N/A'}"
[L64] parts.append(block)
[L65]
[L66] return "\n\n---\n\n".join(parts)

[L271] + selected = {node.id}
[L272] +
[L273] + # Greedily allocate remaining budget to children
[L274] + children = sorted(forest.children(node),
[L275] + key=lambda c: c.utility / max(c.token_cost, 1),
[L276] + reverse=True)
[L277] + for child in children:
[L278] + if child_budget >= child.token_cost:
[L279] + cu, cs = solve(child, child_budget)
[L280] + total_util += cu
[L281] + selected |= cs
[L282] + child_budget -= sum(forest.get_node(n).token_cost for n in cs)
[L283] +
[L284] + if total_util > best[0]:
[L285] + best = (total_util, selected)
[L286] +
[L287] + dp[(node.id, remaining_budget)] = best
[L288] + return best
[L289] +
[L290] + return solve(root, budget)
[L291]
[L292]
[L293] --[L294]
[L295] ### 3.5 CRITICAL: Undefined `node_level` for Unplaced Nodes (PDFs 1, 3)
[L296]
[L297] **The Bug:** CPG++ and PRE use `node_level(q)` to filter candidates by abstraction distance. But `q`
[L298]
[L299] **Fix:** Estimate abstraction level from textual features before placement:
[L300]
[L301]

[L302] def estimate_abstraction_level(node):
[L303] """Heuristic: more abstract concepts have shorter names,
[L304] broader definitions, and appear in more documents."""
[L305] score = 0.0
[L306] score += 1.0 / (len(node.name.split()) + 1) # Shorter = more abstract
[L307] score += len(node.sources) 0.1 # More sources = more general
[L308] score += len(node.children_hints) 0.05 # More sub-concepts = more abstract
[L309] if any(kw in node.definition.lower()
[L310] for kw in ['general', 'category', 'type', 'class', 'family']):
[L311] score += 0.3
[L312] return score

[L353] 1. Extracts knowledge — concepts, definitions, relations, and evidence from raw documents
[L354] 2. Builds a Knowledge Forest — a hierarchy of semantically linked concept nodes organized as rooted trees
[L355] 3. Retrieves knowledge nodes — by traversing the hierarchy (parents, children, cross-links) with adaptive
depth
[L356] 4. Selects context optimally — using a Tree Knapsack algorithm that respects hierarchical precedence
constraints
[L357] 5. Generates verified answers — with claim-level evidence verification and citation binding
[L358] 6. Learns from feedback — a self-evolution loop that updates edge weights based on retrieval success/failure
[L359]
[L360] > Key Insight: Humans organize knowledge by topics and subtopics (e.g., "Computer Science → Operating
Systems → Scheduling → Round Robin"), not by arbitrary text windows. SHIA-RAG mirrors this natural organization
for AI retrieval.

51. Ek line me har step yaad rakho
| Step | Component | Simple Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | Cache | Kya result already available hai? |
| 1 | Intent | User actually kya puch raha hai? |
| 2 | Seed Search | Query se directly relevant concepts kaunse hain? |
| 3 | Adaptive Depth | Kitna deeply explore karna hai? |
| 4 | BFS | Forest me relevant directions me chalo |
| 5 | Tree Knapsack | Limited tokens me best valid context select karo |
| 6 | Context Assembly | Selected knowledge ko LLM-readable format me banao |

if not scores:
return 'UNSUPPORTED', 0.0
avg_score = sum(scores) / len(scores)
if len(scores) >= 2 and max(scores) - min(scores) > 0.4:

return 'CONFLICTING', avg_score
if avg_score > 0.7:
return 'SUPPORTED', avg_score

return 'PARTIAL', avg_score

[L75] > [!IMPORTANT]
[L76] > **Two edge classes solve the Tree-vs-Graph contradiction:**
[L77] > - `HIERARCHICAL` edges form an acyclic forest (enforced by HV)
[L78] > - `SEMANTIC` edges form an unrestricted graph (cycles allowed)
[L79]
[L80]

python
[L81] # Edge class enforcement — applied consistently in all modules
[L82] def validate_edge(edge, forest):
[L83] """Validate edge based on its class."""
[L84] if edge.edge_class == "HIERARCHICAL":
[L85] # MUST be acyclic — check for cycles
[L86] if creates_cycle(edge.source_node, edge.target_node, forest):
[L87] raise CycleError(f"HIERARCHICAL edge {edge.edge_id} would create a cycle")
[L88] # MUST respect single-parent constraint
[L89] validate_single_parent(forest.get_node(edge.target_node), edge.source_node, forest)
[L90] elif edge.edge_class == "SEMANTIC":
[L91] # Cycles are ALLOWED — no acyclicity check needed
[L92] # Just validate that both nodes exist
[L93] assert forest.has_node(edge.source_node)
[L94] assert forest.has_node(edge.target_node)
[L95] else:
[L96] raise ValueError(f"Unknown edge_class: {edge.edge_class}. Must be HIERARCHICAL or SEMANTIC.")

41. Conflict detection me bhi ek subtle issue
Report conflict detect karti hai if:
max(score) - min(score) > 0.4

fileciteturn29file1L221-L230
But score difference ka matlab always factual contradiction nahi hota.
Example:
Evidence A strongly supports claim = 0.95
Evidence B only loosely related = 0.40

Difference:
0.95 - 0.40 = 0.55

System:
CONFLICTING

classify kar sakta hai.
But Evidence B necessarily contradictory nahi hai — maybe sirf irrelevant hai.

Therefore:
High similarity-score variance ≠ guaranteed contradiction.

Ye report ke shown implementation ka critical limitation hai.

20. Example: HELPFUL feedback
Suppose:

feedback signal f = +1

Formula:
\[

\]
So:
\[
w_{new}=1.0\times e^{0.02}
\]
Approximately:
\[
w_{new}\approx1.0202
\]
So weight:
1.0000
↓
1.0202

Yahan numerical example formula ka application hai.
